code.title: Switch: no fall-through, goto case, switch on strings

followUps:
The compiler turns a switch on many string cases into a hash lookup, not a long chain of comparisons. For a small number of cases (about 6 or fewer) it emits plain if/== comparisons; above that it computes the string's hash, jumps to the matching bucket, and confirms with one string.Equals.

So 50 cases cost roughly one hash plus one comparison, not 50 comparisons. The comparison is ordinal, so "A" does not match "a".

Use if/else when the conditions are not simple matches on one value: ranges combined with other variables, different variables per branch, or side-effecting checks. Example: if (age >= 18 && hasId) mixes two variables, which a switch cannot express cleanly.

It is also clearer for one or two branches, and for early-return guard clauses. A switch shines when many branches test the same value; with two branches it is just noise.

code.title: Pass by value vs ref for value and reference types

followUps:
Nothing needed for mutation, but ref lets the method replace the caller's whole list. Without it, list = new List<int>() inside the method only changes the local copy of the reference, while list.Add(1) changes the shared object.

void Reset(ref List<int> l) { l = new List<int>(); }
var x = new List<int>{1,2};
Reset(ref x); // x is now empty and a different object

Because a reference-type argument is a copy of a reference, and both copies point at the same object on the heap. Calling list.Add(5) or setting obj.Name = "x" goes through that reference to the one shared object, so the caller sees it.

ref is only needed when you want to change which object the caller's variable points to (or to pass a value type by alias, for example a swap of two ints).

code.title: Returning a maybe: out, tuple-like pair, exception

followUps:
Because an async method returns before it finishes, and out parameters must be assigned before the method returns. The compiler turns an async method into a state machine whose locals live on the heap, and a ref-like out alias to the caller's stack variable cannot safely outlive the first await.

Return the result through the task instead: Task<(bool Ok, int Value)> or Task<int?>.

It lets you declare the variable right inside the call: int.TryParse(s, out var n) replaces a separate line int n; before it. The variable's scope is the enclosing block, so you can use n on the next lines.

if (int.TryParse("42", out var n))
    Console.WriteLine(n + 1); // 43

Use out _ to discard a value you do not need. It is only a syntax convenience; the compiled code is the same.

code.title: Defensive copy of a mutable struct, and passing by reference

followUps:
A defensive copy is a hidden copy the compiler makes of a struct so a method call cannot change your original. When you call a non-readonly member on an in parameter (or a readonly field) of a mutable struct, the compiler cannot prove the member leaves the data alone, so it copies the struct first and calls the member on the copy.

That copy is exactly the cost in was meant to avoid. Marking the struct readonly struct removes it.

Write a benchmark that calls both versions in a tight loop and let BenchmarkDotNet measure them, with [MemoryDiagnoser] and a Release build. It handles warm-up, JIT tiering and statistics that a hand-made Stopwatch loop gets wrong.

Compare the mean time of ByValue(big) and ByIn(in big) for sizes like 8, 32 and 64 bytes. Expect in to win only for the larger, readonly structs; for a 4-byte struct it is often slower.

code.title: Overload resolution surprises

followUps:
CS0121 is the "call is ambiguous" error: two overloads are equally good and the compiler will not guess. Example: with F(int, long) and F(long, int), the call F(1, 1) converts int to long in a different argument for each, so neither is better in every argument.

Fix it by casting an argument (F(1, 1L)) or by removing or renaming one overload.

Optional parameters are only considered after the argument match, and a candidate that needs no default values wins a tie. So given M(int a) and M(int a, int b = 0), the call M(1) picks M(int a), the one with no omitted arguments.

Overloads that differ only by an optional parameter are confusing and, when both are equally good, can still produce an ambiguity error. Prefer clear overloads over mixing the two.

code.title: Optional parameter defaults are chosen by static type

followUps:
Add a new overload with the extra parameter and keep the old signature, forwarding to it. Changing the existing method breaks callers compiled against the old signature (MissingMethodException at runtime).

public void Save(string path) => Save(path, false);
public void Save(string path, bool overwrite) { ... }

Old binaries keep working, new code gets the option, and the default lives inside the library, so it can change later without recompiling callers.

The options pattern passes one settings object instead of many parameters: Save(path, new SaveOptions { Overwrite = true }). New settings are added as properties with defaults, so the method signature never changes.

It keeps public APIs binary compatible, reads clearly at the call site (names, not positional bools), and is the basis of IOptions<T> in ASP.NET Core configuration.

code.title: Rectangular vs jagged arrays

followUps:
A new int[1000][] with every row created allocates 1001 objects: one outer array of 1000 references plus 1000 row arrays. Each is its own heap object with its own header.

A rectangular new int[1000, N] would be one object. That is also why jagged arrays put more pressure on the garbage collector and are less cache friendly than a flat array.

It exists mainly for historical reasons: it let a string[] be passed to a method taking object[] before generics existed. The rule is that if Dog converts to Animal, then Dog[] converts to Animal[].

It is unsafe: Animal[] a = new Dog[1]; a[0] = new Cat(); compiles but throws ArrayTypeMismatchException, because every store into a reference array checks the real element type. This is the cost of covariance.

code.title: Immutable strings: results must be assigned

followUps:
Interning means the runtime keeps one shared copy of each distinct string literal in a pool, so equal literals are the same object. "net" written twice in your code is stored once, and comparing them by reference is true.

Compile-time literals are interned automatically; runtime-built strings are not, unless you call string.Intern(s). It saves memory for many repeats, but interned strings live until the process ends, so do not intern user data.

Yes, with unsafe code or pointers you can overwrite the characters in place, but it is dangerous because the runtime assumes strings never change. Literals are interned, so changing one changes every use of that literal in the process.

Dictionary keys would also end up in the wrong bucket after the change, and it breaks thread safety. Treat strings as read-only; use string.Create or Span<char> to fill a new one safely.

code.title: Ordinal vs ignore-case comparison and sorting

followUps:
The Turkish I problem: in the Turkish culture, uppercase of i is the dotted İ, not I, and lowercase of I is the dotless ı. So "title".ToUpper() on a Turkish machine does not give "TITLE".

A check like s.ToUpper() == "FILE" then fails only on Turkish systems. Fix it with ToUpperInvariant() or, better, string.Equals(a, b, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase).

It uses a hash function that ignores case, so "HELLO" and "hello" land in the same bucket. The comparer's GetHashCode folds each char to its upper-case form by ordinal rules (no culture) before mixing it into the hash, and Equals compares with the same folding.

Lookups stay O(1) on average. The cost is a slightly slower hash than plain Ordinal, since each character is mapped first.

code.title: StringBuilder vs repeated concatenation

followUps:
Because the builder is a linked list of chunks, and sb[i] must walk the chunk list from the end to find the chunk that holds index i. That is O(number of chunks), not O(1).

For a builder with, say, 100 chunks of 8,000 chars, a loop reading every index does about 100 steps per access. Avoid it: call ToString() once and index the string, or iterate with GetChunks().

In modern .NET (6+), an interpolated string passed to Append is compiled to an interpolated string handler. The pieces are appended straight into the builder, one call each (AppendLiteral, AppendFormatted), so no temporary string is created.

Before .NET 6 it first built a full temporary string with string.Format and then appended it, which means one extra allocation per call.

code.title: In-order traversal with an explicit stack (no recursion)

followUps:
Use a stack of nodes to remember where you came from: go left as far as possible, pushing each node; pop and visit it; then move to its right child.

Stack<Node> st = new(); Node cur = root;
while (cur != null || st.Count > 0) {
  while (cur != null) { st.Push(cur); cur = cur.Left; }
  cur = st.Pop(); Visit(cur);
  cur = cur.Right;
}

Time O(n), space O(h) on the heap, so a tree 100,000 deep cannot overflow the call stack.

Because by the time the stack overflows, the runtime has no stack left to run the exception-handling code on, and the state of the thread is no longer trustworthy. So the process is terminated immediately and no catch or finally runs.

You must prevent it: limit recursion depth, convert to a loop with an explicit Stack<T>, or start a thread with a bigger stack. RuntimeHelpers.EnsureSufficientExecutionStack() throws a catchable InsufficientExecutionStackException before the limit is hit.

code.title: Slicing: array copy vs ArraySegment view

followUps:
Make the type expose a public Length (or Count) property and a Slice(int start, int length) method; the compiler then lets callers write x[1..3], which becomes x.Slice(1, 2). Add an int indexer too, and x[^1] works as x[x.Length - 1].

public int Length => n;
public int this[int i] => data[i];
public MyList Slice(int s, int len) => new MyList(data, s, len);

This is "implicit" support. Alternatively add indexers taking Index and Range directly.

Because ^0 means "zero from the end", which is position Length, one past the last element. Valid indices go to Length - 1, so x[^0] is rewritten to x[x.Length] and throws IndexOutOfRangeException.

Example: for an array of 5 items, ^1 is index 4 (last) and ^5 is index 0 (first), but ^0 is index 5, which does not exist. It is valid only as a range end: a[2..^0] means "from 2 to the end".

code.title: params builds an array at each call

followUps:
You get a NullReferenceException inside the method when it reads the array. Sum(null) matches the normal form: the null is passed directly as the int[], not wrapped in a one-element array.

To pass a single null element you would need an array of nullable or object values. A guard such as if (values == null) throw new ArgumentNullException(nameof(values)); gives a clearer error, but Sum() still gives an empty array, not null.

Each overload avoids a params object[] allocation, boxing of value types, and a slow generic path. Console.WriteLine(int), (string), (double) and so on call the right Write directly, while WriteLine(string format, object arg0, ...) takes up to 3 arguments without an array.

Only when you pass 4 or more arguments does the params object[] overload run, and each int is boxed into a heap object. The many overloads are a performance optimisation for a very hot method.

code.title: Cutting allocations in a log formatter

followUps:
It generates a fast, strongly typed logging method at compile time. You declare a partial method with [LoggerMessage(EventId = 1, Level = LogLevel.Information, Message = "Order {Id} shipped")], and the source generator writes the body.

The generated code checks IsEnabled first, caches the message template, and passes typed values without boxing or a params object[]. The string is only formatted if a provider actually writes the message, so a disabled level costs almost nothing.

Watch the Gen0 collection rate and the allocation rate. In production, dotnet-counters monitor shows Gen 0 GC Count and Allocation Rate, and you can also read GC.CollectionCount(0) and GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread().

As a rough sign of trouble, hundreds of Gen0 collections per second, or a high "% time in GC" counter, mean heavy short-lived allocation. Then use an allocation profiler (dotnet-trace, PerfView, or Visual Studio) to find which call sites allocate.
